headline: US and China establish diplomatic relations
summary: On 1 January 1979 the United States and the People's Republic of China formally established diplomatic relations, and Washington ended official relations with Taiwan.
significance: Normalization completed the opening begun by Nixon and aligned Washington and Beijing against Moscow. Soviet media treated it as an anti-Soviet combination.

headline: Czechoslovakia splits into two states
summary: At midnight on 1 January 1993 Czechoslovakia ceased to exist, peacefully dividing into the Czech Republic and Slovakia.
significance: The 'Velvet Divorce' was a rare negotiated break-up of a state, in sharp contrast to Yugoslavia's wars. It redrew Central Europe a little over three years after the fall of communism.

headline: Zapatista rebels seize towns in Chiapas
summary: On 1 January 1994, the day NAFTA took effect, the Zapatista National Liberation Army seized San Cristobal de las Casas and other towns in the Mexican state of Chiapas.
significance: The rising was timed to the start of the North American Free Trade Agreement and put Mexico's indigenous south and its ruling party under international scrutiny. It opened a year of crisis for Mexico, Washington's new free-trade partner.

headline: Russia frees prices: shock therapy begins
summary: On 2 January 1992 the Russian government lifted state controls on most consumer prices, the opening move of Yegor Gaidar's economic reform.
significance: Prices multiplied within weeks, wiping out savings and making the reform programme politically explosive. It set the terms of Russia's turbulent transition to a market economy.

headline: Noriega surrenders to US forces
summary: On 3 January 1990 Panamanian strongman Manuel Noriega, who had taken refuge in the Vatican nunciature after the US invasion, surrendered to American troops and was flown to Miami to face drug charges.
significance: Noriega had for years been a paid US intelligence asset before becoming an indictment target. His capture ended Operation Just Cause and raised enduring questions about Washington's dealings with him.

headline: Bush and Yeltsin sign START II
summary: On 3 January 1993 Presidents George Bush and Boris Yeltsin signed the START II treaty in Moscow, agreeing to cut strategic nuclear warheads by about two-thirds and eliminate land-based multiple-warhead missiles.
significance: It was the deepest arms-reduction agreement yet negotiated, signed weeks before Bush left office. Its ratification became entangled in Russian domestic politics.

headline: Carter imposes grain embargo on the USSR
summary: On 4 January 1980 President Carter announced a partial embargo on grain sales to the Soviet Union and other measures in response to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
significance: The embargo marked the end of detente in practical terms. It also hurt American farmers and was lifted by Reagan in 1981.

headline: US Navy F-14s shoot down two Libyan MiGs
summary: On 4 January 1989 two US Navy F-14s from the carrier John F. Kennedy shot down two Libyan MiG-23 fighters over the Mediterranean off Libya.
significance: It came amid US charges that Libya was building a chemical-weapons plant at Rabta. Tripoli called the jets unarmed reconnaissance planes; Washington said they had acted with hostile intent.

headline: Hamas bombmaker Yahya Ayyash killed by booby-trapped phone
summary: On 5 January 1996 Yahya Ayyash, the Hamas bombmaker known as 'the Engineer', was killed in Gaza when an explosive-laden mobile phone detonated as he took a call; Israel's Shin Bet was widely held responsible.
significance: Ayyash had built the bombs for a wave of suicide attacks in Israel. His killing was followed by a deadly Hamas bombing campaign in February and March 1996 that reshaped Israeli politics.

headline: Georgian President Gamsakhurdia flees Tbilisi
summary: On 6 January 1992 Georgia's President Zviad Gamsakhurdia fled Tbilisi after two weeks of fighting with armed opposition forces besieging his government building.
significance: His ouster opened the way for Eduard Shevardnadze's return and years of civil conflict in Georgia. It was one of the first violent changes of power in the post-Soviet states.

headline: Manila apartment fire exposes the Bojinka plot
summary: On 6 January 1995 a chemical fire in a Manila apartment led police to bomb-making materials and a laptop belonging to Ramzi Yousef's cell, exposing plans to kill the Pope and bomb US airliners over the Pacific.
significance: The discovery foiled what became known as the Bojinka plot and led to Yousef's arrest a month later. Elements of the plan prefigured the September 11 attacks.

headline: Vietnamese forces take Phnom Penh
summary: On 7 January 1979 Vietnamese troops and Cambodian rebels captured Phnom Penh, ending the Khmer Rouge regime of Pol Pot.
significance: The invasion ended a regime responsible for mass killing but installed a Hanoi-backed government that China, ASEAN and the US refused to recognize. Weeks later China attacked Vietnam.

headline: Bosnian deputy premier shot dead under UN escort
summary: On 8 January 1993 Bosnian Deputy Prime Minister Hakija Turajlic was shot dead by a Serb soldier at a checkpoint near Sarajevo while riding in a UN armoured vehicle.
significance: The killing, in the custody of UN peacekeepers, became a symbol of the UN's inability to protect anyone in Bosnia. It came as the Geneva peace talks were under way.

headline: Francois Mitterrand dies
summary: On 8 January 1996 former French President Francois Mitterrand died in Paris, eight months after leaving office.
significance: Mitterrand had led France for fourteen years, through the end of the Cold War, German unification and the Maastricht treaty.

headline: Baker and Tariq Aziz meet in Geneva
summary: On 9 January 1991 US Secretary of State James Baker and Iraqi Foreign Minister Tariq Aziz met in Geneva for over six hours; Aziz refused to accept a letter from President Bush to Saddam Hussein.
significance: It was the last high-level attempt to avert war before the UN's 15 January deadline for Iraq to leave Kuwait.

headline: Bosnian Serbs proclaim their own republic
summary: On 9 January 1992 Bosnian Serb leaders proclaimed a Serb republic within Bosnia-Hercegovina.
significance: The proclamation prefigured the partition of Bosnia and the war that began three months later.

headline: FMLN launches 'final offensive' in El Salvador
summary: On 10 January 1981 the FMLN guerrillas launched what they called a final offensive against the Salvadoran government, days before Ronald Reagan took office.
significance: The offensive failed to topple the government but began a decade of full-scale civil war. It led the outgoing Carter administration to resume military aid and made El Salvador a central front of Reagan's Central America policy.

headline: Soviet troops seize buildings in Vilnius
summary: On 11 January 1991 Soviet troops seized the press building and other sites in Vilnius as Moscow moved against Lithuania's independence government.
significance: The seizures were the prelude to the bloody storming of the Vilnius television tower two days later, which ended hopes that Gorbachev would let the Baltic republics go peacefully.

headline: Algeria's President Chadli resigns under army pressure
summary: On 11 January 1992 Algerian President Chadli Bendjedid resigned; the army then cancelled the second round of elections the Islamic Salvation Front was poised to win.
significance: The military's intervention plunged Algeria into a decade of civil war that killed well over 100,000 people.

headline: Congress authorizes war against Iraq
summary: On 12 January 1991 the US Congress voted to authorize the use of force to expel Iraq from Kuwait.
significance: The votes gave President Bush domestic backing for war three days before the UN deadline.

headline: Civil war erupts in South Yemen
summary: On 13 January 1986 a shoot-out at a Politburo meeting in Aden began a short, bloody civil war within South Yemen's ruling Marxist party.
significance: Thousands were killed in less than two weeks, and Soviet citizens had to be evacuated. The conflict weakened Moscow's only Marxist client state in the Arab world.

headline: Soviet troops storm the Vilnius TV tower
summary: Early on 13 January 1991 Soviet troops and tanks stormed the television tower in Vilnius, killing fourteen civilians.
significance: The 'Bloody Sunday' crackdown hardened Baltic resolve and Western opposition to Moscow's use of force. It discredited Gorbachev's claimed ignorance of the operation.

headline: US, Russia and Ukraine agree to remove Ukraine's nuclear arms
summary: On 14 January 1994 Presidents Clinton, Yeltsin and Kravchuk signed a trilateral statement in Moscow under which Ukraine would give up the nuclear weapons left on its soil by the USSR.
significance: The agreement settled one of the gravest proliferation risks of the Soviet collapse. Ukraine's security assurances were formalized later in the Budapest Memorandum.

headline: Crowds storm Stasi headquarters in East Berlin
summary: On 15 January 1990 demonstrators broke into the East German Ministry for State Security headquarters on Normannenstrasse in East Berlin.
significance: The storming came amid fears that the Stasi was destroying its files. The archive that survived later let millions of East Germans read what had been gathered on them.

headline: European Community recognizes Croatia and Slovenia
summary: On 15 January 1992 the European Community member states recognized Croatia and Slovenia as independent states.
significance: Recognition, pressed by Germany, marked the international end of Yugoslavia and turned attention to Bosnia.

headline: The Shah leaves Iran
summary: On 16 January 1979 Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi left Iran, ostensibly on vacation, amid months of mass protest.
significance: He never returned. His departure cleared the way for Ayatollah Khomeini's return and the collapse of America's closest ally in the Gulf, with heavy costs for US intelligence and policy in the region.

headline: El Salvador peace accords signed in Mexico City
summary: On 16 January 1992 the Salvadoran government and the FMLN signed peace agreements at Chapultepec Castle in Mexico City, ending a twelve-year civil war.
significance: The UN-brokered accords ended one of the bloodiest Cold War conflicts in the hemisphere, in which Washington had backed the government.

headline: Operation Desert Storm air war begins
summary: In the early hours of 17 January 1991, Baghdad time, US-led coalition aircraft and cruise missiles began attacking Iraq.
significance: The air campaign opened the war to liberate Kuwait and displayed precision weapons and stealth aircraft to the world.

headline: Earthquake devastates Kobe
summary: On 17 January 1995 a magnitude 6.9 earthquake struck the Kobe region of Japan, killing more than 6,000 people.
significance: It was Japan's deadliest earthquake since 1923, and the slow official response shook confidence in the Japanese government.

headline: Iraqi Scuds hit Israel
summary: Early on 18 January 1991 Iraq fired Scud missiles at Tel Aviv and Haifa.
significance: Saddam Hussein aimed to draw Israel into the war and split the Arab members of the coalition. Washington pressed Israel not to retaliate and rushed Patriot batteries to it.

headline: Algiers Accords signed to free US hostages
summary: On 19 January 1981 the United States and Iran, through Algerian mediation, signed the Algiers Accords providing for the release of the American hostages and the unfreezing of Iranian assets.
significance: The agreement ended fourteen months of negotiations over the hostages seized at the US Embassy in Tehran.

headline: US hostages freed from Iran
summary: On 20 January 1981, minutes after Ronald Reagan was sworn in, the 52 Americans held in Iran for 444 days were flown out of Tehran.
significance: The hostage crisis had broken Carter's presidency and changed US policy toward Iran for decades. Among the hostages were CIA officers whose presence Iran had used as propaganda.

headline: Terry Waite disappears in Beirut
summary: On 20 January 1987 Terry Waite, the Archbishop of Canterbury's envoy who had been negotiating for the release of Western hostages, was seized in Beirut.
significance: Waite had unknowingly been entangled in the arms-for-hostages dealings exposed weeks earlier as the Iran-Contra affair. He was held for nearly five years.

headline: Soviet troops storm Baku
summary: In the night of 19-20 January 1990 Soviet troops forced their way into Baku under a state of emergency, killing more than a hundred people.
significance: The crackdown, ordered after anti-Armenian pogroms and a nationalist challenge to Communist rule, turned Azerbaijani opinion decisively against Moscow.

headline: UN demands Libya hand over Lockerbie suspects
summary: On 21 January 1992 the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 731, urging Libya to respond to US, British and French requests concerning the bombings of Pan Am 103 and UTA 772.
significance: The two suspects in the Lockerbie bombing were alleged to be Libyan intelligence officers. Libya's refusal led to UN sanctions in March 1992.

headline: Sakharov exiled to Gorky
summary: On 22 January 1980 the dissident physicist Andrei Sakharov was detained in Moscow and sent into internal exile in the closed city of Gorky.
significance: His banishment, weeks after the Afghanistan invasion, symbolized the Brezhnev regime's crackdown on dissent. Gorbachev released him in December 1986.

headline: Guerrillas attack La Tablada barracks in Argentina
summary: On 23 January 1989 members of the leftist Movimiento Todos por la Patria attacked the army barracks at La Tablada near Buenos Aires; the army retook it after over a day of fighting.
significance: The bloody attack, the last of its kind in Argentina, strengthened the military's hand against the civilian government of Raul Alfonsin.

headline: Soviet nuclear-powered satellite crashes in Canada
summary: On 24 January 1978 the Soviet ocean-surveillance satellite Cosmos 954 re-entered the atmosphere and scattered radioactive debris across Canada's Northwest Territories.
significance: The reactor-powered reconnaissance satellite exposed the hazards of military surveillance in space and led to a joint US-Canadian clean-up operation.

headline: Gunman kills two outside CIA headquarters
summary: On 25 January 1993 a gunman opened fire on cars waiting to enter CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia, killing two agency employees.
significance: The killer, Mir Aimal Kasi, fled to Pakistan and was captured there in 1997. The attack was an early sign of anti-American terrorism linked to the Afghan war's aftermath.

headline: Norwegian research rocket triggers Russian nuclear alert
summary: On 25 January 1995 Russian early-warning radar detected a Norwegian scientific rocket launched from Andoya, and President Yeltsin's nuclear briefcase was activated.
significance: Norway had notified Russia of the launch, but the warning never reached the right people. It was among the most dangerous false alarms of the nuclear age.

headline: Havel elected first president of the Czech Republic
summary: On 26 January 1993 the Czech parliament elected Vaclav Havel the first president of the independent Czech Republic.
significance: The dissident playwright had led the Velvet Revolution and was the last president of Czechoslovakia.

headline: Freed hostages welcomed home in Washington
summary: On 27 January 1981 the 52 Americans released by Iran arrived in Washington and were welcomed by President Reagan at the White House.
significance: Reagan used the occasion to warn that future acts of terrorism against Americans would meet swift and effective retribution.

headline: Six US diplomats escape Iran with Canadian help
summary: On 28 January 1980 six American diplomats who had evaded capture when the US Embassy was seized flew out of Tehran on Canadian passports.
significance: The 'Canadian caper', publicly credited to Canada's embassy, was a joint operation with the CIA, whose role was declassified only in 1997.

headline: Space shuttle Challenger explodes
summary: On 28 January 1986 the space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing all seven crew.
significance: The disaster grounded the shuttle fleet for nearly three years and delayed US military and reconnaissance satellite launches.

headline: Deng Xiaoping begins US visit
summary: On 29 January 1979 Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping began an official visit to Washington, the first by a PRC leader.
significance: Deng's visit followed normalization and preceded China's attack on Vietnam by weeks. Moscow watched for an anti-Soviet alignment.

headline: Iraqi forces attack Khafji
summary: On the night of 29 January 1991 Iraqi forces crossed into Saudi Arabia and occupied the town of Khafji; Saudi, Qatari and US forces retook it by 1 February.
significance: It was the only major Iraqi ground offensive of the Gulf War.

headline: France announces end of nuclear testing
summary: On 29 January 1996 President Jacques Chirac announced that France had permanently ended nuclear testing after a final series in the South Pacific.
significance: The resumed tests of 1995 had provoked worldwide protest. France then backed the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty signed later in 1996.

headline: Car bomb kills dozens in Algiers
summary: On 30 January 1995 a car bomb exploded outside the central police station in Algiers, killing more than forty people.
significance: It was one of the deadliest single attacks of Algeria's civil war.

headline: Spanish Embassy burned in Guatemala City
summary: On 31 January 1980 Guatemalan police stormed the Spanish Embassy, which had been occupied by peasant protesters; a fire killed 37 people, and Spain broke relations.
significance: The massacre became a defining atrocity of Guatemala's civil war; the only peasant survivor was later abducted from hospital and killed.

headline: McDonald's opens in Moscow
summary: On 31 January 1990 the first McDonald's in the Soviet Union opened on Pushkin Square in Moscow.
significance: Thousands queued on opening day. The restaurant became a symbol of perestroika's opening to the West.
